title: After Christendom
subtitle: The era the reader is standing in. The dechurching, the deconstruction, the reckonings, and the end of the church's home-field advantage in the West, written from inside, with the ending unwritten.

sections.title: Forty Million Quiet Departures
sections.body:
Every other essay in this library describes an era with an ending. This one does not have an ending yet. It is written from inside the thing it describes, by a pastor serving a church in the middle of it, which means it is written without the one advantage every historian enjoys, knowing how it turned out. Treat what follows accordingly: not a verdict of history but a report from the middle of the night, filed by a man who is also in the dark. Some of it will look wrong in fifty years. The task is to be honest now anyway.

Begin with the fact that frames everything else. In the last quarter century, about forty million American adults stopped attending church. The figure comes from The Great Dechurching, the 2023 study by pastors Jim Davis and Michael Graham with the political scientist Ryan Burge, and the authors describe it as the largest and fastest religious shift in the country's history, more people gone, they reckon, than came into the churches during the First and Second Great Awakenings and the Billy Graham crusades combined. By 2021 the Pew Research Center found that 29 percent of American adults claimed no religious affiliation at all, the people the surveys call the nones. And the detail that should haunt pastors more than either figure is the study's own finding about how the leaving happened. Most of the departed did not storm out over doctrine or scandal. They moved, changed jobs, had a child, fell out of the habit, found Sunday easier without it, and one year quietly became ten. The door did not slam. It simply never opened again. And the study's stranger finding sits beside that one: many of the departed told the researchers they remained open to returning. The leaving was quiet. So, apparently, is the waiting.

The deeper account of what happened is not on any survey. The philosopher Charles Taylor spent A Secular Age, in 2007, describing the change underneath the change: not that the arguments against God suddenly improved, but that the conditions of belief shifted. Five centuries ago in the West, belief in God was the default setting of an entire civilization, the air a person breathed whether or not he loved it. Now belief is one option among many, contested, fragile, chosen, and it feels that way even to those of us who hold it. Taylor names the modern condition the immanent frame, a world that seems to run, plausibly and completely, without reference to anything beyond itself. Christendom was the long arrangement in which the surrounding culture carried the faith: the calendar, the laws, the schools, the assumptions, all leaning toward the church, so that attending was respectable and staying home required an explanation. That arrangement is what has ended in the West. The culture has set the faith down. Whether that is a death or a deliverance is the question this whole era is asking, and this essay will not pretend the answer is settled. But one distinction can be made at the start and held to the end. What is over is not the church. What is over is the tailwind.

sections.title: Taking the Faith Apart in Public
sections.body:
Around the middle of the 2010s a word migrated from philosophy seminars into church lobbies: deconstruction. What it named was not new, believers have always lost their faith or fought through it, but the form was new. Deconstruction now happened in public, on podcasts and in hashtags and memoirs, with an audience, and the audience made it a genre. A generation raised in the evangelical subculture began taking that inheritance apart piece by piece, on the record, and calling itself exvangelical. Then 2019 became the marker year. Joshua Harris, who in his early twenties had written I Kissed Dating Goodbye, the 1997 manual that taught a generation of church kids to treat romance as contamination waiting to happen, had already repudiated the book and asked its publisher to stop printing it. That summer he announced publicly that his marriage was ending and that, by every measure he knew, he was no longer a Christian. Other prominent names followed, songwriters, authors, pastors, and each announcement was cheered by one crowd and jeered by another, both crowds missing the grief at the center of it.

Honor the grief, because much of what was dismantled deserved to be dismantled. The purity culture Harris repented of writing had loaded shame onto teenagers where the gospel puts grace, and its bill came due in marriages and counseling rooms for twenty years. The political captivity was real. The scandals, which take the next section, were real. And the thin catechesis of the attractional years was real: children raised on Moralistic Therapeutic Deism, the nice god with no demands that the sociologist Christian Smith documented in 2005, did not have much to lose, and when the nice god stopped being useful they concluded, reasonably, that they had outgrown him. Hear the indictment inside that. Many deconstructors did not betray their formation. They completed it. A faith presented as useful will be discarded as useless, and we were the ones who presented it that way. I was one of the ones. The deconstruction wave is, among other things, the attractional era's invoice, arriving a generation late and addressed to the children.

But honoring the grief is not the same as following it all the way down, and this platform's conviction, stated here as history because the era itself is starting to show it, is that deconstruction honored honestly is still only demolition, and demolition is not a dwelling. Taking apart the inherited thing can name what was false. It builds nothing to live in. The interesting figures of this era are the ones who kept digging after the drywall came down, past the American additions, past the political captures, past the marketing, and struck something older: creed, canon, the church of the long centuries. Tearing down to the ground and digging down to the foundation look identical for the first several feet. They are not the same act. One ends in an empty lot. The other is how you find out what was load-bearing all along. The era has both crews working, and from the street it is still hard to tell them apart. For those who stopped and walked away, the right response is grief without contempt, because the thing they left was often the counterfeit they said it was. The door stays lit. The rest of this essay follows the ones still digging.

sections.title: Trust, Audited
sections.body:
No account of the era's exits can be honest without this section, and no section of this essay is heavier to write. The revelations came in waves and across every tradition. In 2002 the Boston Globe documented the sexual abuse of children by Catholic priests and, worse, the system that had quietly moved abusers from parish to parish. In 2018 a Pennsylvania grand jury laid out decades of the same pattern across that state's dioceses. In 2019 the Houston Chronicle documented abuse and concealment across Southern Baptist churches, where congregational independence had let accused men move between pulpits. In 2022 an independent investigation that the Southern Baptist Convention itself had commissioned reported that denominational leaders had for years kept a private list of accused ministers while telling survivors and churches that nothing could be done. Prominent ministries and megachurches watched founders resign under investigation, some exposed only after their deaths. These are not rumors. They are public records, many of them produced by the institutions themselves once denial ran out.

Name the pattern precisely, because the pattern, not the existence of sinners, is what the era cannot forgive. It was never news that the church contains sin; the church has confessed as much about itself from the beginning, and a world that had actually heard the doctrine of sin should not have been shocked to find it in pews and pulpits. What broke trust was the second, colder thing: institutions that, when the wounded came forward, moved to protect the institution. The lawyers before the lambs. The brand before the body. Reputations managed while children paid. The watching world drew the reasonable conclusion that some shepherds cared for the sheep the way a rancher does, as assets. And I cannot write that sentence from outside it. I hold a title, pastor, that for generations opened doors on trust the holder had not personally earned. That unearned trust is gone now. My generation inherited its benefits and watched men of our own guild burn it down, and if I am honest, the deference was never good for us. Its loss, whatever else it is, is a severe mercy. It leaves us only what the first churches had: lives that either commend the gospel or do not.

So refuse the comfortable telling on both sides. The world did not primarily reject a holiness it found too demanding. It rejected a hypocrisy it found too familiar. And yet the rejection itself borrows the church's own standard, because the outrage assumes that shepherds must not devour sheep, which is Ezekiel's cry against Israel's shepherds before it is any newspaper's. Scripture is not surprised by any of this, and it locates the courtroom exactly where this era has: "For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God" (1 Peter 4:17). The reckonings, whatever the motives of every party carrying them, have functioned as precisely that, judgment beginning at the house of God. The only faithful response on record anywhere in the book is not reputation management. It is repentance, the public kind, the costly kind, the kind that sides with the wounded because their Shepherd does.

sections.title: The Accelerant
sections.body:
Then the buildings closed. In March 2020 a pandemic did what no persecution in American history had done, emptied nearly every church in the country in a single month, and Easter that year was preached to cameras in vacant rooms. The closures themselves are not the story here; the church has endured plagues before and will again. The story is what reopening revealed. Attendance did not return to what it had been. Some of the missing had died. Some had drifted to the congregation down the road with the different mask policy. But a large share had simply discovered, in the enforced experiment, that they did not miss it, that the habit had been interrupted and underneath the habit there was nothing else holding. The pandemic built almost nothing and destroyed almost nothing. It revealed. It was the stress test the era had not scheduled, and what stood on habit came down, and what stood on conviction held.

The same months revealed something harder about the church's inner life. Congregations that had never needed to say aloud what they were discovered, under the pressure of closures and masks and a poisonous election, that they were two or three congregations wearing one name. Members left leftward, convinced their church had baptized cruelty. Members left rightward, convinced their church had bowed to Caesar's health department. Pastors, whatever they did, were accused from both directions in the same week, and nobody who watched those years is surprised at how many of them quietly left ministry when it was over. The pandemic did not create the fractures. It stripped the paint off them. And the livestream, adopted in an emergency, stayed, teaching a generation that worship is also available as content, one open tab among many, consumable at convenience with the kettle on. The attractional era had turned the congregation into an audience. The pandemic made the audience optional.

Yet the same experiment ran the other direction too, and honesty requires both results. Some believers discovered in those months exactly what could not be streamed: the bread and the cup, the hand on a shoulder, the voices of other sinners in a room carrying the parts of the creed you could not say that week, the funeral you attend with your whole body or not at all. The ones who returned came back knowing why they had. A sifting like that is a grief and a clarification at once, and the church that emerged from it was smaller, sadder, and considerably less deceived about itself.

Historians will argue over the measurements for decades; pastors lived the shape of it, and the shape was compression. Years of slow drift happened in about two. Everything this essay has described so far, the dechurching, the deconstruction, the collapse of assumed trust, was already moving before 2020. The pandemic was the accelerant poured across all of it at once, and when the smoke cleared, the American church could no longer pretend the old arrangement was merely aging. It was over, and everyone had seen the room with the lights on.

sections.title: The Flag and the Cause
sections.body:
On January 6, 2021, a crowd broke into the United States Capitol to stop the certification of an election, and among the banners it carried were crosses, Christian flags, and the name of Jesus, and when the Senate chamber was seized, a prayer was offered aloud from the rostrum. Whatever else that day was, it was a religious image the whole world saw, and the church that produced it owes the world an account. Start with the steelman, because the fears underneath it are not fake. Many American Christians look at the last half century and see real losses: institutions that once at least respected their faith now openly contemptuous of it, their children catechized by screens and schools into creeds nobody voted on, convictions their grandparents shared with the whole culture reclassified as bigotry within a single generation. The grief is legitimate, and any account that sneers at it has already failed. Christian nationalism is the answer chosen for that grief, the promise that the right man, the right party, the right law can secure what only the cross secures. This platform calls it what the older tradition would call it: not conservatism, not patriotism, but idolatry, the cross conscripted into a flag. A Christianity that believes it must hold the Capitol has already confessed that it does not believe Christ holds the throne.

Now turn the same instrument the other direction, with the same grief. The opposite capture rarely carries flags into buildings, because it does not conscript the faith; it dissolves it. Here the church is not seized for a nation but reduced to a cause: congregations where the creed thinned decade by decade until what remained was the moral energy of whichever movement the culture supplied that year, with Jesus retained as mascot; sins renamed or quietly unnamed when naming them would cost standing with the side; the resurrection demoted to metaphor, because metaphors ask nothing. Its steelman is also real. These believers watched the church wrap itself in a flag, watched cruelty done in Christ's name, and resolved to be nothing like that, and the compassion is not the error. The error is the same error as the other capture, the faith made useful, its worth measured by its service to a program the world wrote first. The old mainline denominations ran that experiment for three generations, and their emptied buildings are its published results. Subtract the offense of the gospel and you subtract, eventually, the reason to come.

I write neither of those paragraphs from a distance. I have felt both pulls from the inside: the ache to be protected by power when my people are mocked, and the ache to be approved by the culture when my convictions embarrass me at dinner. They are the same offer at different counters, relevance in exchange for the cross. And Scripture already staged this scene. Joshua, outside Jericho, meets a figure with a drawn sword and asks the only question politics knows how to ask: "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?" The answer he receives is the whole matter: "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come" (Joshua 5:13-14). No. The Lord does not enlist. Both captures, the flag and the cause, are attempts to enlist him, and both end in the same place, a church that has traded away the only thing it carried that the world did not already have.

sections.title: The Rival Catechist
sections.body:
While the church argued about all of the above, formation moved. The smartphone arrived in 2007, and within a decade it was in nearly every pocket and bedroom in the country. Understand what that means in this library's terms. Catechesis is not a classroom program; it is whatever forms a person's loves, habits, and attention, hour by repeated hour, and by that definition the algorithmic feed is the most effective catechist ever built. It knows its pupil individually. It adjusts to him in real time. It disciples him toward outrage, envy, distraction, and the endless audit of his own image, and it holds class for hours a day, every day, beginning in childhood. A church that sees its people for one hour a week, and fewer of them after 2020, is no longer the primary religious formation in its own members' lives, whatever the sign out front claims. That sentence is as true of my congregation as of any other, and as true of my own phone as of any teenager's.

The costs are no longer speculative. The social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, in The Anxious Generation in 2024, assembled the evidence that childhood itself was rewired in the early 2010s, play-based childhood giving way to phone-based childhood, and that this great rewiring, his phrase for it, tracks with a surge of anxiety, depression, and fragility among the young across the developed world. Haidt does not write as a churchman, and the platform's rule for secular findings applies to him as to everyone: he has the symptom right and the anthropology short. What he documents as a mental health crisis, the older tradition would also name a formation crisis, souls trained from childhood by a liturgy of glass, and formed by it exactly the way liturgies always form. The nones did not stop being catechized when they stopped attending. They changed catechists.

The church's first instinct, and I shared it, was to compete on the algorithm's terms: stream the service, brand the pastor, cut the sermon into clips, win the attention auction. The attractional instinct, migrating online with its logic intact. Some of that is simple faithfulness to where people actually are; Paul used the roads Rome built. But nobody should mistake the roads for neutral ground, and I say this as a man publishing these words onto a screen, into the same contest for your attention that I am indicting. The indictment includes the instrument, and the writer holding it. The open question of the era, and it is genuinely open, is whether communities of embodied practice, table and font, confession and neighbor, the unrecorded hour, can form people more deeply than the feed malforms them. More hangs on that answer than on any election this era will hold. The early signs, which are the business of the final sections, point somewhere older than anyone expected.

sections.title: Christendom Ends Here, Not Everywhere
sections.body:
Now widen the lens, because the era looks entirely different from almost anywhere else on earth. In 2002 the historian Philip Jenkins published The Next Christendom and set before Western readers a fact missionaries had known for a generation: the center of gravity of the Christian faith has moved south and east. The churches of Africa, Latin America, and much of Asia are full and growing, and the representative Christian of this century, Jenkins argued, is not a white man in a Western suburb but a poor woman in the global South. While European sanctuaries were being converted into apartments and concert venues, some of the fullest churches in Europe's own capitals were being planted by African missionaries, the mission field of the nineteenth century sending pastors back to the countries that once sent them. Whatever is dying in the West, it is not Christianity.

That reframe should discipline every sentence a Western Christian writes about decline, including every sentence in this essay. The funeral we keep rehearsing is not the faith's funeral; it is Christendom's, and only the local branch of Christendom at that. The longer history steadies the nerves further, because the faith has changed addresses before. It was born on Asia's western edge, prayed in Aramaic and Greek and Syriac long before it prayed in Latin, and was African before most of Europe had heard the name of Christ. North Africa, the land of Athanasius and Augustine and for centuries the theological engine room of the whole church, has held only a remnant of Christians for more than a thousand years. Asia Minor, home to every one of the seven churches of Revelation, is not a Christian land today. The church wept at each loss, and the faith did not die. It moved, carried by exiles and merchants and mothers, and it kept the covenant rather than the real estate. Nothing in the gospel promises any nation a permanent Christian majority. Something in the gospel promises that the church will outlast the gates of hell, and the church, at this hour, counted across the whole earth, is larger, more southern, and less white than it has ever been. Perhaps the strangest mercy of this era is that American Christians are being handed, without choosing it, the ordinary situation of the worldwide church, the minority condition in which the faith was born and in which most Christians who have ever lived have lived. We are not pioneers of some unprecedented darkness. We are latecomers to normal.

God was never a Western possession. Christendom was a Western arrangement. The confusion of those two sentences built empires, funded mission boards, and eventually produced the panic this era swims in, and the global church stands as the living correction of it. Christendom is ending here. It is not ending everywhere, and where it never existed, the church never needed it.

sections.title: Houses in Babylon
sections.body:
And now the countersigns, reported carefully, because they are observations rather than statistics, and this essay promised not to blur that line. Pastors, priests, and journalists keep filing the same reports from different directions: young adults arriving at liturgical churches nobody marketed to them, asking for the old things by name, confession, kneeling, the church calendar, fasting, catechism; congregations finding that it is the demanding hour, not the convenient one, that the young keep attending; a quiet turn among ordinary believers toward the church fathers, the creeds, the traditions with long memories. The counting is not done, and honesty forbids announcing a revival. But the direction of the hunger is hard to miss, and it runs opposite to every assumption the attractional era trained into us. The generation we tried to win by lowering the threshold appears to be looking for a threshold worth crossing.

The scholars arrived at the same door from the other side. In 2016 the historian Alan Kreider published The Patient Ferment of the Early Church, an account of how the faith grew in the centuries when it had no buildings, no stages, no legal standing, and no strategy any modern consultant would recognize, and the book found an audience of pastors, I am one of them, who a generation earlier would have been handed marketing. Kreider's early church did not attract; it formed. Its worship was closed to outsiders. Its catechesis took years. Its growth was slow, unplanned, and by every account unstoppable, and what drew the watching pagan world was not an event but a people, patient under pressure, strange in their mercy, unafraid to die. The era that watched Christendom die went looking for the church that had never had it, and found there not a technique but a temperament. Patience. The one virtue no growth strategy ever budgeted for.

Which brings the era to its text, the one the church keeps rediscovering in every exile because it was written to exiles. In the sixth century before Christ, the prophet Jeremiah sent a letter to the people of Judah who had been carried off to Babylon, a people whose temple was rubble, whose national arrangement with God appeared to be finished, and whose own prophets kept promising that the exile would be brief and the furniture soon restored. Jeremiah wrote the opposite. "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease. But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:4-7). Read that as the assignment, because the Western church has been handed the exiles' situation, and the letter rules out both of the church's favorite plans. Not restoration: there is no marching on Babylon in it, no scheme for retaking the old arrangement, and the same chapter names the prophets promising a quick return as liars. Not assimilation: the exiles are to remain unmistakably the people of God in the middle of the city, praying to the LORD, multiplying, refusing Babylon's gods whatever the furnace costs, as Daniel's friends would soon demonstrate. What remains is the third thing, the hard thing, what the sociologist James Davison Hunter in 2010 called faithful presence: build, plant, marry, raise children, work, pray, and seek the good of the very city that carried you off, your welfare bound up with its welfare, for seventy years if it takes seventy years.

So here is the thesis of this essay, and the conviction under this whole library: what is dying in the West is Christendom's furniture, not Christ's church. The tailwind is gone, the deference is gone, the assumed belief and the cultural carry and the full parking lot are going or gone, and every one of those was furniture. None of it was the house. "I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:18) was said to a movement of a few dozen with no buildings at all, and it has outlasted every arrangement made since, and it will outlast ours. But I will not end by resolving what is not resolved. I am writing from inside the exile, not after it. I do not know how long this era runs, or what name the historians will give it, or whether the countersigns of this section become its next chapter or only a footnote. The historian who writes this era's ending has not been born. What I know is the assignment while the ending stays unwritten, because the assignment is in the letter: houses, gardens, marriages, children, prayer, and the welfare of a city that did not ask for us and does not believe it needs us. The exiles who obeyed that letter buried their grief in Babylon's soil and planted gardens over it, and their grandchildren walked home singing songs that had been written in the land where everyone said the faith would die. Whether we become that kind of exile, whether I do, whether the church you can see from your own street does, is not a question an essay can settle. It is being settled now, in the era you are standing in, one house, one garden, one ordinary Tuesday at a time.

keyFigures.name: Charles Taylor
keyFigures.note: Philosopher whose A Secular Age (2007) described belief's shift from the default of a civilization to one contested option among many.

keyFigures.name: Philip Jenkins
keyFigures.note: Historian whose The Next Christendom (2002) showed the faith's center of gravity moving to Africa, Latin America, and Asia.

keyFigures.name: Jim Davis and Michael Graham
keyFigures.note: Pastors who, with the political scientist Ryan Burge, documented the dechurching of about forty million Americans (2023).

keyFigures.name: Joshua Harris
keyFigures.note: Author of a defining purity-culture manual who publicly repudiated the book, and then the faith, in 2019, the deconstruction wave's most visible figure.

keyFigures.name: Jonathan Haidt
keyFigures.note: Social psychologist whose The Anxious Generation (2024) traced the rewiring of childhood by the phone-based life.

keyFigures.name: Alan Kreider
keyFigures.note: Historian whose The Patient Ferment of the Early Church (2016) handed post-Christendom pastors the pre-Christendom church.
